course.title: SOLID Principles: Writing Clean, Maintainable Code
course.shortDescription: Master the five SOLID principles of object-oriented design to write better, more maintainable software.
course.description:
Learn the fundamental SOLID principles that form the foundation of clean, maintainable object-oriented code.

**What You'll Learn:**
• Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
• Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
• Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
• Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
• Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

**Perfect For:**
• Software developers wanting to improve code quality
• Teams adopting clean code practices
• Anyone preparing for technical interviews
• Developers transitioning to OOP
learningOutcomes: Apply SOLID principles in real-world projects
Write more maintainable and testable code
Recognize code smells and refactor effectively
Improve code quality and team collaboration

chapters.title: Introduction to SOLID Principles
chapters.description: Understanding the importance of SOLID principles in software design

lessons.title: What are SOLID Principles?
lessons.description: Introduction to the five SOLID principles and their importance

data.text:
SOLID is an acronym for five design principles intended to make software designs more understandable, flexible, and maintainable:

• **S**ingle Responsibility Principle
• **O**pen/Closed Principle
• **L**iskov Substitution Principle
• **I**nterface Segregation Principle
• **D**ependency Inversion Principle

These principles were introduced by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob) and have become fundamental to object-oriented design.

chapters.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
chapters.description: A class should have only one reason to change

lessons.title: Understanding SRP
lessons.description: Learn what single responsibility means and why it matters

data.text:
**Definition:** A class should have only one reason to change.

**Key Concepts:**
• Each class should focus on a single task or responsibility
• Changes to one responsibility shouldn't affect others
• Promotes high cohesion and low coupling

**Benefits:**
• Easier to understand and maintain
• Reduces the risk of breaking existing functionality
• Improves testability
• Facilitates code reuse

chapters.title: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
chapters.description: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification

lessons.title: Understanding OCP
lessons.description: Learn how to extend functionality without modifying existing code

data.text:
**Definition:** Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

**Key Concepts:**
• Add new functionality without changing existing code
• Use abstraction and polymorphism
• Protect stable code from changes

**Implementation Strategies:**
• Inheritance and polymorphism
• Strategy pattern
• Decorator pattern
• Dependency injection

chapters.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
chapters.description: Objects should be replaceable with instances of their subtypes

lessons.title: Understanding LSP
lessons.description: Learn about proper inheritance and substitutability

data.text:
**Definition:** Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without breaking the application.

**Key Concepts:**
• Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types
• Derived classes must not break base class contracts
• Preserve expected behavior

**Common Violations:**
• Strengthening preconditions
• Weakening postconditions
• Throwing new exceptions
• Changing expected behavior

chapters.title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
chapters.description: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use

lessons.title: Understanding ISP
lessons.description: Learn how to design focused, client-specific interfaces

data.text:
**Definition:** No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.

**Key Concepts:**
• Create small, focused interfaces
• Split large interfaces into smaller ones
• Clients depend only on what they need

**Benefits:**
• Reduces coupling
• Improves code clarity
• Makes systems more flexible
• Easier to refactor and maintain

lessons.title: Understanding DIP
lessons.description: Learn how to invert dependencies for better flexibility

data.text:
**Definition:** High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

**Key Concepts:**
• Depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete implementations
• Invert the direction of dependencies
• Use dependency injection

**Benefits:**
• Reduces coupling between modules
• Makes code more testable
• Facilitates parallel development
• Improves flexibility and maintainability
